title: the goddess in Kamsa's hands
hookLine: Kamsa grabs the eighth child, and she rises from his hands as the Goddess
carry: shakti: divine power, worshiped as the goddess

lines: "IT'S A GIRL. LEAVE ME THIS ONE."
cards: A newborn cries in the cell. The guards jerk awake and run to the king. Kamsa leaps out of bed, the Bhagavata says, hair loose, stumbling, and rushes to the prison.
This is the eighth child, the one the voice warned him about at the wedding. Devaki holds the baby close and begs him. It's a girl, a daughter of your own house.
Don't kill a girl. You've taken so many of my children. Leave me just this one.
Kamsa doesn't hear her. He tears the child out of her arms.

teach.b: He swings the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his grip. She rises into the air, and she is no longer a baby.
The Bhagavata calls her the younger sister of Vishnu: a goddess with eight arms, holding weapons, in garlands and bright clothes. And she speaks down to him. What will you gain by killing me, fool?
The one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Stop killing the helpless. Then she is gone.
Kamsa frees Devaki and Vasudeva and even weeps, but by morning his ministers talk him into hunting newborns. He heard the truth, and chose fear. So who was she?
The Bhagavata has already told us.
Before the birth, Vishnu sent her, his own power, Yogamaya, and said people on earth would worship her under many names: Durga, Bhadrakali, Vaishnavi, Chandika, Ambika and more.
Here is a big Hindu teaching hiding in a prison cell.

teach.h: SHAKTI: DIVINE POWER, WORSHIPED AS THE GODDESS
teach.b: Many Hindus call God's power shakti, and worship that power as the Goddess. The Lord and his shakti aren't rivals, and Krishna's story and Durga's aren't two separate worlds.
The Devi Mahatmya, the Goddess's own great text, says it too: she would be born to Yashoda, in Nanda's house.
That's why one family can keep Janmashtami in late summer and Navaratri in the fall, and bow to the same divine power in both: the power that protects, and that no tyrant can hold in his hands.

how: Hindus who follow the Bhagavata honor the girl born to Yashoda as Yogamaya, a form of the Goddess; many devotees identify her with Vindhyavasini, the Goddess of the Vindhya hills, and many families keep both Janmashtami and Navaratri.

the goddess tells Kamsa his killer is already born
somewhere else, she says, and she tells him to stop killing the helpless.
in Hindu teaching, Vishnu and the Goddess are rivals
in the Bhagavata, Vishnu himself sends her, his own power, and says she'll be worshiped as Durga and more.

games.q: your little cousin Rohan asks why Durga turns up in the story of Krishna's birth. what do you tell him?
o: the girl was Vishnu's own power, the Goddess; God and his shakti work together.
two different stories got mixed up by mistake.
Durga came down to fight baby Krishna.
games.why: the Bhagavata has Vishnu send Yogamaya and name her Durga, Ambika and more: his power, worshiped as the Goddess.

practice: Sit tall and steady. Many Hindus call on the Goddess with one name, said again and again. Choose one from today: Durga, or Ambika, which means Mother.

Say it slowly on each out-breath, and picture the girl rising free from Kamsa's hands. If you don't pray, name one fear that keeps steering you, and let your grip on it loosen, the way she slipped from his.

wordCard.voice: Yogamaya. The Lord's own power, born as Yashoda's daughter, who rises from Kamsa's hands as a goddess and tells him the truth.

orig.note: yogamaya: the Lord's own power, born as Yashoda's daughter, who rises from Kamsa's hands.

carryVoice: Your line: shakti, divine power, worshiped as the Goddess. Tomorrow, a stranger comes to Gokula. That's day eight hundred eighty-four.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.4: the guards wake, Devaki's plea, the girl slips from Kamsa's hands and appears as the eight-armed goddess, her words, Kamsa's remorse, the ministers' counsel
Bhagavata Purana 10.2.6–12: Vishnu sends Yogamaya to be born to Yashoda and names the forms under which she will be worshiped (Durga, Bhadrakali, Vaishnavi, Chandika, Ambika and others)
Devi Mahatmya 11 (Markandeya Purana): the Goddess foretells her birth to Yashoda in Nanda's house and her dwelling in the Vindhya hills
